title: What Space Does to Your Body (And What Happens When You Come Home)
description:
Within two days in orbit, astronauts can grow up to three percent taller. That is just the start: here is what weightlessness does to your fluids, bones, muscles, eyes and even your genes, based on NASA research including the famous Twins Study.

Sources:
- NASA, The Human Body in Space: https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/the-human-body-in-space/
- NASA, Twins Study Results Published in Science Journal (2019): https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/nasas-twins-study-results-published-in-science-journal/
- NASA, Twins Study overview: https://www.nasa.gov/humans-in-space/twins-study/
- NASA, Astronaut Exercise: https://www.nasa.gov/missions/station/iss-research/astronaut-exercise
- NASA Technical Reports Server, Seated height and spinal elongation in microgravity: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/20090007782

This video is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice.

scenes.narration: Two hundred forty miles above your head, the human body starts rebuilding itself. Within two days, you could even be taller.
scenes.headline: SPACE REBUILDS YOUR BODY

visual.query: astronaut floating inside International Space Station cupola
visual.note: astronaut floating weightless inside the station

scenes.narration: Every system in your body grew up under one constant force: gravity. It pulls your blood toward your feet, presses down on your spine, and loads your bones every time you stand. Now imagine that force switched off.
scenes.headline: BUILT FOR GRAVITY

visual.query: person standing on mountain summit sunrise
visual.note: a person standing upright outdoors, feet firmly on the ground

scenes.narration: That is daily life on the International Space Station, which orbits about two hundred forty miles above Earth. Astronauts there are not weightless because gravity is gone. They are falling around the planet nonstop, so their bodies never feel their own weight.
scenes.headline: FALLING AROUND EARTH

visual.query: International Space Station over Earth
visual.note: the space station orbiting above Earth

scenes.narration: The first change happens fast. On Earth, your body constantly works to keep fluid from pooling in your legs. In orbit, that system keeps pushing upward, with nothing pulling back. So body fluids shift toward your chest and head.
scenes.headline: FLUIDS RUSH TO YOUR HEAD

visual.spec: two human outlines side by side: on Earth fluid concentrated in the legs, in orbit fluid shifted up toward chest and head, with arrows

scenes.narration: Your spine changes too. With no weight pressing down, your back relaxes and lengthens. NASA research found that in as little as two days, a typical crew member can grow up to three percent taller. For a six foot person, that is about two inches.
scenes.headline: UP TO 3% TALLER
scenes.sub: In as little as two days

visual.query: human vertebral column lateral view illustration Gray's Anatomy
visual.note: side view of the human spine and its discs

scenes.narration: But that bonus height is temporary, and it comes with a catch. Your body is a careful accountant. Whatever it stops using, it stops paying to maintain. And in weightlessness, it stops using a lot.
scenes.headline: USE IT OR LOSE IT

visual.query: astronaut portrait inside space station module
visual.note: astronaut floating with tools and cables around

scenes.narration: Start with your bones. They are living tissue, constantly broken down and rebuilt to match the loads they carry. In space, weight-bearing bones like your hips and legs lose on average one to one and a half percent of their mineral density every month.
scenes.headline: BONES LOSE DENSITY

visual.query: human femur hip bone anatomy illustration
visual.note: the hip and thigh bone, weight-bearing bones

scenes.narration: Over a six month mission, that adds up. And those minerals have to go somewhere. Extra calcium leaves the body through the kidneys, and together with dehydration, that raises the risk of kidney stones.
scenes.headline: WHERE THE CALCIUM GOES

visual.query: human kidney anatomy illustration
visual.note: simple kidney anatomy illustration

scenes.narration: Your muscles follow the same logic. On Earth, your legs and back fight gravity all day just to keep you upright. In orbit, they barely work. Without exercise and good nutrition, astronauts lose muscle mass faster than they would on the ground.
scenes.headline: MUSCLES SHRINK TOO

visual.query: human leg muscles anatomy illustration
visual.note: muscles of the legs and back that hold you upright

scenes.narration: So astronauts train like it is their job, because it is. Crew members average about two hours of exercise every day, on a treadmill, a stationary bike, and a resistance machine that uses pistons and a flywheel to mimic lifting weights where nothing weighs anything.
scenes.headline: TWO HOURS OF EXERCISE DAILY

visual.query: astronaut exercising ARED advanced resistive exercise device
visual.note: astronaut lifting on the resistive exercise machine

scenes.narration: Bones and muscles you might see coming. But some of the strangest changes happen deep inside your cells. And NASA had the perfect way to measure them: an astronaut with an identical twin.
scenes.headline: THE ASTRONAUT WITH A TWIN

visual.query: Scott Kelly Mark Kelly twins study
visual.note: identical twin astronauts Scott and Mark Kelly together

scenes.narration: Astronaut Scott Kelly spent nearly a year aboard the space station. His identical twin, Mark Kelly, also an astronaut, stayed on Earth. Because the brothers share the same genes, ten research teams could compare them and isolate what spaceflight itself had changed.
scenes.headline: ONE IN SPACE, ONE HOME

visual.query: Scott Kelly year in space ISS
visual.note: Scott Kelly aboard the space station

scenes.narration: Scott's gene activity shifted in orbit as his body adapted. His gut bacteria changed. His telomeres, the protective caps on the ends of chromosomes, behaved in unexpected ways. And researchers saw signs of inflammation and a thickening of the wall of his carotid artery, in his neck.
scenes.headline: CHANGES DOWN TO YOUR GENES

visual.query: telomeres chromosome ends fluorescence microscopy
visual.note: chromosomes with glowing telomere caps at the ends

scenes.narration: Even his appetite surprised the scientists. Scott ate about thirty percent fewer calories than researchers had anticipated, and his body mass dropped by seven percent during the flight.
scenes.headline: FEWER CALORIES, LESS MASS

visual.query: astronauts eating food space station galley
visual.note: astronauts sharing a meal with floating food packets

scenes.narration: Then there are the eyes. That upward shift of fluid may press on the eyes, and some astronauts come home with changes to their vision. In space, Scott's blood showed higher levels of a protein involved in how the body handles water.
scenes.headline: PRESSURE ON YOUR EYES

visual.query: astronaut eye exam ocular health space station
visual.note: astronaut having an eye examination in orbit

scenes.narration: Here is the part most people never think about. For many astronauts, one of the hardest moments of the whole mission is not launch. It is coming home.
scenes.headline: THE HARD PART: COMING HOME

visual.query: Soyuz capsule landing parachute Kazakhstan
visual.note: a crew capsule descending under its parachute

scenes.narration: After months in orbit, your heart and blood vessels have adjusted to a world where blood does not drain toward your feet. Returning astronauts can feel lightheaded when they stand, and some even faint.
scenes.headline: STANDING UP GETS HARD

visual.query: astronaut helped out of capsule after landing
visual.note: recovery crew helping an astronaut after landing

scenes.narration: Your brain needs time to readjust too. In the Twins Study, Scott's thinking speed and accuracy held steady in orbit, but they dipped after landing, and some of that decline was still there six months later.
scenes.headline: THE BRAIN READJUSTS

visual.query: human brain MRI side view
visual.note: a side view brain scan

scenes.narration: The good news is how much bounces back. About ninety one percent of Scott's gene expression changes returned to normal after he landed. His gut bacteria, weight and immune responses largely recovered, and a flu vaccine he received in space worked just as it should.
scenes.headline: MOST OF IT BOUNCES BACK

visual.query: Scott Kelly Mark Kelly after landing
visual.note: the twin brothers reunited after the mission

scenes.narration: A few changes did linger, though, and bone is the slow one. NASA notes that bone lost in space may not fully return, even with rehabilitation.
scenes.headline: BONE IS THE SLOW ONE

visual.query: bone density scan DEXA image
visual.note: a bone density scan image

scenes.narration: And one hazard cannot be solved with a treadmill. Space is filled with radiation, including galactic cosmic rays that are very hard to shield against. The health risks are mostly long term, and researchers believe some DNA damage seen in Scott came from radiation exposure.
scenes.headline: THE INVISIBLE HAZARD

visual.query: galactic cosmic rays radiation illustration
visual.note: artist illustration of cosmic radiation streaming past a spacecraft

scenes.narration: Now stretch everything you just heard into a trip to Mars. Mars is on average about one hundred forty million miles away. The journey takes about six months of weightlessness, and a message home can take up to twenty minutes each way.
scenes.headline: NOW MAKE IT MARS

visual.query: Mars global view Viking orbiter mosaic
visual.note: the planet Mars seen from space

scenes.narration: Once you land, gravity is only about one third of Earth's, and each day is about thirty seven minutes longer. Future missions to the Moon and deep space could last up to three years.
scenes.headline: ONE THIRD GRAVITY

visual.query: astronauts Mars surface concept art habitat
visual.note: artist concept of astronauts working on Mars

scenes.narration: And that is the real takeaway. Your body is not a fixed machine. It is constantly reading the forces around it and rebuilding itself to match. Take gravity away, and it adapts within days. Bring gravity back, and it slowly adapts again.
scenes.headline: YOUR BODY ADAPTS

visual.query: Earth from space Blue Marble
visual.note: the whole Earth seen from space

scenes.narration: Which means that right now, just by standing and walking around, you are giving your bones and muscles a reason to stay strong. Gravity is not only holding you down. It is quietly keeping you built.
scenes.headline: GRAVITY KEEPS YOU BUILT

visual.query: people walking city sidewalk daylight
visual.note: people walking along a sunny city street

scenes.narration: Follow Inside Your Body for more of the science of you.
